Presentation Abstract

Program#/Poster#: 800.09/BBB40
Presentation Title: Neural correlates of reinforcement learning in the human substantia nigra as measured by the local ﬁeld potential
Location: Hall F-J
Presentation time: Wednesday, Oct 17, 2012, 8:00 AM - 9:00 AM
Authors: A. G. RAMAYYA1, *K. A. ZAGHLOUL4, B. C. LEGA2, C. T. WEIDEMANN5, G. H. BALTUCH2, M. J. KAHANA3;
1Neurosci. Grad. Group, 2Neurosurg., 3Psychology, Univ. of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA; 4Surgical Neurol. Br., Natl. Inst. of Neurolog. Disorders and Stroke, NIH, Bethesda, MD; 5Psychology, Univ. of Swansea, Swansea, United Kingdom
Abstract: Understanding the neural mechanisms that support reinforcement learning is of great importance to the [[unable to display character: ﬁ]]eld of neuroscience. While much has been learned about how the activity of single neurons relates to learning, relatively little is known about the population-level correlates of this behavior. Here, we obtain local [[unable to display character: ﬁ]]eld potential recordings from the SN of Parkinson[[unable to display character: ʼ]]s Disease patients undergoing surgery for the implantation of a deep brain stimulator to characterize the role of population-level activity in the SN during reinforcement learning. We identify two behaviorally-relevant neural signals. First, we [[unable to display character: ﬁ]]nd increased high frequency power (78-137 Hz) and decreased low frequency power (5-6 Hz) shortly following feedback presentation during unexpected reward when compared to all other conditions, which may reflect a representation or reward prediction error. Second, increased alpha power shortly prior to feedback presentation (11-12 Hz) and stimulus presentation (6-8 Hz) when the participant is expecting a reward compared to when they are expecting a loss, which may be a representation of reward expectation. Our [[unable to display character: ﬁ]]ndings advance our current understanding of the role of the SN in reinforcement learning.
Disclosures:  A.G. Ramayya: None. K.A. Zaghloul: None. B.C. Lega: None. C.T. Weidemann: None. G.H. Baltuch: None. M.J. Kahana: None.

Presentation Abstract

Program#/Poster#: 746.04/D27
Presentation Title: The spatial structure of hippocampal theta rhythms reflects behavioral state
Location: Hall F-J
Presentation time: Wednesday, Oct 17, 2012, 11:00 AM -12:00 PM
Authors: *F. T. SOMMER1, G. BUZSAKI2, G. AGARWAL1;
1Univ. California, Helen Wills Neurosci Inst., Redwood Ctr. Theoret Neurosci, BERKELEY, CA; 2New York Univ., New York, NY
Abstract: The theta rhythm is a prominent hippocampal oscillation that may serve as a reference for decoding the activity of neurons known as place cells. One salient property of this rhythm is that it is spatially inhomogeneous in phase and amplitude. However, current models of hippocampal physiology and function are largely based on the idea of a single, global theta oscillation. By characterizing the spatial variations, we may better understand the generative process underlying the theta rhythm(s), as well as the functional consequences of spatial variation upon the neural code.
We analyze the theta rhythm measured at multiple sites within region CA1 in freely-moving rats. Using methods of dimensionality reduction and demodulation, we identify the defining spatio-temporal properties of the theta rhythm.
We find that the spatial variations in the CA1 LFP lie largely within a subspace of two complex dimensions. The first dimension of this subspace captures the average structure of the theta rhythm, manifesting as a traveling wave that propagates radially across the apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells; the second dimension represents deviations from this average structure in relative phase and amplitude. Demodulation of these two oscillating
components reveals two slowly varying time courses (termed A1 and A2). Interestingly, A1 and A2 are correlated with different aspects of behavior for rats running on a linear track: A1 is correlated to rat velocity, while
A2 covaries with rat position. Furthermore, the trial-by-trial variations of this modulation are predicted by the ongoing activity of single neurons.
In conclusion, the spatio-temporal structure of theta oscillations in CA1 can be described by two components, each of which corresponds to a different behavioral variable.

OSCILLATION

Presentation Abstract

Program#/Poster#: 203.14/CCC23
Presentation Title: Medial entorhinal cortical neurons exhibit temporally-modulated firing patterns during stationary treadmill running
Location: Hall F-J
Presentation time: Sunday, Oct 14, 2012, 9:00 AM -10:00 AM
Authors: *B. J. KRAUS1, M. P. BRANDON1,2, M. A. CONNERNEY1, R. J. ROBINSON, II1, S. ERIKSSON1, C. P. LIBBY1, J. A. WHITE1,3, M. E. HASSELMO1, H. EICHENBAUM1;
1Ctr. for Memory and Brain, Boston Univ., BOSTON, MA; 2Div. of Biol. Sci., UC San Diego, La Jolla, CA; 3Dept. of Bioengineering, Brain Inst., Univ. of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT
Abstract: Neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) exhibit spatially-modulated firing patterns when rats are allowed to forage for food distributed randomly within an open enclosure, including grid cells firing in a repeated array of spatial locations. Grid cell firing can be modeled with input consisting of speed and heading, generating firing at regular intervals of spatial distance. As the MEC is a dominant source of input into the hippocampus, many models hypothesize that the outputs from grid cells are used by the hippocampus to generate place cells in support of spatial cognition and memory. However, several recent findings have reported temporally modulated firing by hippocampal neurons (“time cells”), suggesting a role in the temporal organization of memories. Here we asked whether the MEC is also involved in temporal processing. In the absence of speed and heading input, the grid cell model will generate firing at regular time intervals. To determine if MEC neurons fire at regular intervals of distance or time, rats were trained on a figure-eight maze that included a motorized treadmill in the center stem, allowing us to observe firing patterns as rats ran in place over time. To dissociate between coding for time versus distance on the treadmill, the speed of the treadmill on each trial was randomly selected from within a predetermined range, while either the total distance traveled or the time spent on the treadmill was held constant across trials within each recording session. To determine the spatial firing properties of the same neurons, their activity was also recorded as the rats foraged for food pellets in an open field, allowing us to identify each neuron as a grid cell, conjunctive grid-by-head direction cell, head direction cell, or boundary vector cell.
Many MEC neurons exhibited temporally modulated firing patterns during treadmill running. Some neurons had a single well-defined temporal firing field, whereas other neurons had multiple distinct temporal firing fields, and the firing rates of yet other neurons ramped up or down during the treadmill running period. Most striking was evidence of periodic firing among a subset of MEC neurons; with periods ranging from 1-10 s. Preliminary analysis did not reveal any reliable relationship between the temporal firing patterns observed during treadmill running and the type of spatial firing patterns observed during foraging. In addition, the firing patterns of some MEC neurons were best correlated with time on the treadmill, whereas that of others was best correlated with distance. These findings suggest that both MEC and hippocampal neurons code for temporal as well as spatial and other environmental regularities.

Presentation Abstract

Program#/Poster#: 279.3/EE62
Title: Neural correlates of context-based models of free recall
Location: South Hall A
Presentation Time: Sunday, Oct 18, 2009, 3:00 PM - 4:00 PM
Authors: *J. R. MANNING, S. M. POLYN, M. J. KAHANA;
Univ. Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA
Abstract: The free recall paradigm has been employed by memory researchers for over a century, and has led to the discovery of a number of important behavioral trends in the sequences of recalls that subjects make. These trends are thought to reflect fundamental neural mechanisms underlying encoding and recall. A number of computational models attempt to explain how these mechanisms might be implemented. For example, context-based models posit the existence of a neural representation of the context in which words are studied. According to this class of models, the context representation changes gradually over the study period of the experiment. During the recall period, the reinstatement of the context representation plays a critical role in determining the sequence of recalls. Here we recorded intracranially from human neurosurgical patients as they studied and freely recalled lists of words. We found a candidate neural representation of context which changed gradually as the patients studied the lists. Consistent with context-based models, this gradually changing activity was reinstated just prior to each recall. Taken together, our findings provide neural support for context-based models.
